Marcus Veld 5 min read · Just now -- Listen Share It was the first tab I opened, before email, before Slack, every single morning for over a year. I told myself it was diligence. It was something else. Press enter or click to view image in full size For a little over a year, the first thing I did most mornings, before coffee had finished brewing, was open our biggest competitor’s changelog and public roadmap. I told myself this was basic competitive diligence the kind of thing a responsible founder does. It took an honest conversation with my co-founder, and a slightly embarrassing moment of self-recognition, to understand that it wasn’t diligence at all. It was a way of avoiding my own to-do list by feeling productively anxious about someone else’s. The numbers: Mornings, out of roughly 260 working days, this was the first thing I checked: ~230 Average time spent on it per morning: 12–15 minutes Times a competitor’s shipped feature actually changed a decision we made: 2, in over a year Time since I stopped the daily habit: 7 weeks Times I’ve missed it: fewer than I expected What it actually looked like The ritual was consistent enough that I could describe it in my sleep. Open the changelog. Read every entry since yesterday. Open their public roadmap board, scan for anything new. Open their pricing page, just to check nothing had shifted overnight. Sometimes a quick scroll through their most recent public-facing content, a blog post, a LinkedIn update from their founder looking for tone, positioning, anything that felt like a signal. By the time I closed the last tab, twelve or fifteen minutes had passed, and I hadn’t yet looked at our own product, our own metrics, or the actual list of things I’d said, the night before, that I’d do first thing this morning. The conversation that named it My co-founder noticed the pattern before I consciously did — she pointed out, half-joking, that she could tell how our week was going by how long I spent on “competitor rounds” each morning. Slow weeks for us, longer rounds. Weeks where we had real, unambiguous progress to make, shorter ones or skipped entirely. That correlation, once she said it out loud, was uncomfortably accurate and not something I’d ever consciously noticed about myself. “She could tell how our week was going by how long I spent on ‘competitor rounds’ each morning. That correlation was uncomfortably accurate.” The honest version of what was happening: on mornings where I didn’t have a clear, energizing next action of my own, checking the competitor’s changelog gave me something that felt like useful information while actually functioning as a socially acceptable form of procrastination. It felt like work. It generated a small, familiar hit of anxious alertness. It let me postpone opening my own task list by another fifteen minutes, dressed up as competitive awareness. What I got wrong I’d conflated “staying informed about the market” with “checking one specific competitor’s public output daily,” which are very different levels of diligence. Genuinely useful competitive awareness understanding shifts in the broader market, noticing patterns across several players, catching a real strategic move that should change our plans doesn’t require a daily ritual. It requires periodic, deliberate attention, maybe monthly, with actual analysis attached rather than a reflexive morning scroll. I also mistook frequency for rigor. Checking something every single day felt more thorough than checking it once a month, but in practice the daily version produced almost no decisions two, across an entire year, that I can point to as genuinely changed by something I saw in that changelog while the anxious residue of the habit was a daily, low-grade cost that I’d never actually measured against what it was buying me. Timeline: Roughly 14 months ago: Started the habit after a competitor shipped a feature that briefly worried me. The anxiety from that one real moment calcified into a daily ritual. Months 2–12: Ritual becomes automatic, unquestioned, first thing every morning regardless of what else was happening. Month 13: Co-founder names the pattern out loud, half-jokingly, during an unrelated conversation. Week 1 after: Tried simply skipping it for a few mornings, noticed a specific, uncomfortable restlessness not about missing information, about missing the ritual itself. Weeks 2–4: Replaced the daily check with a scheduled monthly review, block on the calendar, actual notes taken, shared with my co-founder afterward. Weeks 5–7: Noticed mornings starting with my own priorities instead of someone else’s shipped features. Harder to quantify, but the shift was real. “The anxious residue of the habit was a daily, low-grade cost I’d never actually measured against what it was buying me.” What I was actually avoiding The uncomfortable answer, once I sat with it honestly, is that the habit spiked hardest during weeks where I didn’t have full confidence in our own direction.
